Q: Change variable to constant during runtime A:

Technically arrays can be both constant and mutable in JS. When an array is declared like const myArray = [], the array can still be modified like myArray.push('Fred'), even though you can't reassign like myArray = {name: 'Fred'}. (note the = assignment operator).

The way to prevent yourself (or someone else) from reassigning the values later is to pass the completed array to Object.freeze().

If the purpose is to flag the value as a constant your code editor, your code editor would have to be pretty smart .

If the purpose is to leverage the superior performance of const, you're likely optimizing too early.

Q: Need help learning when to use conditionals and loops A:

+1 for this comment.
IMHO, this is the most valuable given to you so far, and to be sure you take undertand why you should take your time following it, let me try to phrase it differently.

My impression is that right now, your approach to writing code is:

  1. Understand the problem.
  2. Break it down into a list of instructions for the computer.

You have skipped a step though, namely: Break down the problem into manageable sub-problems.

What happens if we do?
You are trying to find the greatest prime number under some input, which we can break down into:

  1. Get an input from the user to store into int input.
  2. Find the greatest number n <= input that verifies a generic condition.
    int findIf(int upperBound) will do that.
  3. Make that condition "n is prime".
    bool isPrime(int n) will do this part.

The magic that @justin is suggesting you to try is:

  1. Write findIf with a mock version of isPrime (e.g. temporarily make isPrime return true for even numbers, or for multiple of some k)
  2. Test it with hardcoded values of input
  3. Only once that is done, write the actual code for isPrime so that it actually test primality.
  4. The final touch is to change input so that it is not hardcoded anymore.

You will see bricks fall into place nicely with this approach.

Finally, in a few months, when you feel more comfortable with C++, you can learn how to make isPrime a parameter to the findIf function, so findIf truly becomes what its name suggests.

Q: Check if string contains a character in a set? A:

Use exists:

val identifiers = Set('a', 'b', 'c')
val result = input.exists(identifiers.contains)

This checks whether any character in input is contained in identifiers.

Q: Sudden Docker error about "client API version" A:

I was running a Docker in Docker (DinD) container in the Kubernetes cluster, and I recently upgraded it to version 29.1.5-dind. After that upgrade, I started getting the following error:

Error response from daemon: client version 1.41 is too old. Minimum supported API version is 1.44, please upgrade your client to a newer version

I fixed it by setting DOCKER_MIN_API_VERSION to 1.41 in the environment variables.

The new code snippet looks like this:

.
.
.
spec:
  containers:
    - name: docker
      imagePullPolicy: Always
      image: "docker:29.1.5-dind"
      command:
        - dockerd
      args:
        - --host=unix:///var/run/docker.sock
        - --storage-driver=overlay2
        - --mtu=1380
        - --group=999
      env:
        - name: "DOCKER_MIN_API_VERSION"
          value: "1.41"
.
.
.

Reference: blog post Docker Engine v29 - Blog

Q: PyCharm installs pip that don't give any function A:

Start with the basics and [create a project](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/pycharm/creating-empty-project.html) as per PyCharms help. Choose an environment to your liking: virtualenv, conda or uv to setup your python interpreter.

Next make sure to install numpy and other libraries into your created environment. More on that can be found in PyCharms help as well at [the install requirement landing page](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/pycharm/managing-project-dependencies.html).

It is probably easiest to use virtualenv with requirements.txt for simplicity to start with.

Q: Why is processing a sorted array faster than processing an unsorted array? A:

Or perhaps instead of using bit-wise ops, just completely prune away the filtering condition by converting it to a matter of counter frequencies, and doing a dot-product against byte ordinals (pre-requisite being data[i] can only have values in the uint8 range). A major advantage of this approach is that whether array is sorted or not makes no difference, since no meaningful branch prediction is occurring anywhere in the core loop to iterate the input. The index capping filter at the summation is essentially immaterial in any grand scheme of things.

pre-make a counter array one for each byte's ordinal, convert the loop to a mindless one that tracks occurrence of each byte.

++counter_array[data[i]]

If a handy foreach() type construct is available in your particular language, then this can even be iterated through without manually incrementing ++i in the 3rd part of the vanilla for() loop. e.g. if this were in awk instead of C++, then something like

for (_ in data)
    ++counter_array[data[_]]

After iterating the input input, just start at 128, and iterate it to the highest index

for (_ = 128; _ < 256; ++_)
    __ += counter_array[_] * _

And scale it by the 100,000 only once at the return statement. In order to bypass the filtering condition altogether, the summation loop has to be manually incremented (unless you wanna opt for some new age map-reduce construct).
